title: Amanda Vandervort, President of the Gainbridge Super League, steps down
content:
Gainbridge Super League president Amanda Vandervort, who has been with the league since its inception, is set to depart from her role, the United Soccer League announced Monday.

Vandervort will step down Friday “to pursue other opportunities,” the league said. She was named president of the USL Super League in 2021, arriving after nearly two years at FIFPRO and nine years with Major League Soccer.

“From the beginning, we set out to create more opportunities for women in the game and more communities where professional women’s sports are celebrated, and I’m proud of the league we’ve built together,” Vandervort said in a statement.

She went on to say that she was grateful for her time with the organization and the chance to build something new.

“I believe deeply in the people and clubs who will carry the league forward, and I’ll continue to cheer on our incredible teams from the stands. For me, it feels like the right time to close this chapter, and I’m looking forward to what comes next,” Vandervort said.

Paul McDonough, the USL’s president and CEO, credited Vandervort with playing “an important role” in growing women’s soccer at the USL over the last five years, most notably by leading the launch of the Super League. “Building a professional league from the ground up is a major undertaking, and Amanda deserves a lot of credit for her leadership and the work it took to make it happen,” McDonough said in a statement.

Under Vandervort’s leadership, the Super League was awarded Division 1 sanctioning and became the second D1 women’s league in the U.S. when play began in 2024.  The move raised immediate questions over whether the Super League would attempt to compete with the National Women’s Soccer League, which had long operated as the only D1 women’s league in the country.

However, time has proven what Vandervort had long preached: that the league was not aiming to compete with the NWSL. Instead, it has succeeded by expanding professional playing opportunities for players across the U.S., and, by operating as a D1 league, the hope was to minimize the potential for substandard club operations.

Vandevort’s unexpected departure comes at a transitional moment for the Gainbridge Super League, as the league is commercially known.

The Super League just kicked off an abbreviated fall season running from Aug. 15 through Nov. 28, before it transitions to a spring-to-fall calendar in 2027. In June, the league announced it would “flip” its calendar to better align with the NWSL. The abbreviated season will be the league’s third since play started in 2024.

The shift follows another major milestone. In July, the league reached a tentative agreement with its players for their first-ever collective bargaining agreement. Notably, the CBA provides the league with labor stability through the 2031 women’s World Cup.

While the USL Super League has enjoyed relative success in its first two seasons, one of its inaugural clubs, Spokane Zephyr, unexpectedly folded in late May, with ownership announcing it would not return for a third season.
